npm, package.json, and node_modules

Node's package manager and dependency manifest — the equivalent of Composer and composer.json.

Laravel projects lean on Composer: composer.json lists dependencies, composer install downloads them into vendor/. Node's equivalent is npm (bundled with Node itself), package.json as the manifest, and node_modules/ as the download target instead of vendor/.

Figure 1.1 is this project's actual package.json.

// Figure 1.1: the project manifest (package.json)
{
  "name": "support-desk-instructor",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "description": "Support ticketing REST API — teaching case study for Full Stack Development (Back End weeks).",
  "type": "module",
  "main": "src/server.js",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node src/server.js",
    "dev": "node --watch src/server.js",
    "test": "echo \"no tests yet — added in Week 3\" && exit 0"
  },
  "license": "UNLICENSED",
  "dependencies": {
    "dotenv": "^17.4.2",
    "express": "^4.19.2"
  }
}

A few parts worth naming individually:

  • "dependencies" — the packages this project needs at runtime, each pinned with a version range (^4.19.2 means "4.19.2 or a later compatible 4.x"). Running npm install reads this list and downloads everything into node_modules/ — never committed to git (see .gitignore), regenerated on any machine from package.json alone, exactly like vendor/ from composer.json.
  • "scripts" — named shortcuts run via npm run <name> (npm start is a special case that doesn't need run). dev uses Node's built-in --watch flag to restart the server automatically on file changes — the Node equivalent of php artisan serve restarting, without needing an extra package (nodemon) to get it.
  • "type": "module" — tells Node which module system this project's .js files use. That's the very next topic.

You won't hand-edit node_modules/ or usually package.json's dependency list directly — npm install <package> adds a dependency and updates the file for you, the same way composer require does.
